# Ludwigia erecta (L.) H.Hara

First published in J. Jap. Bot. 28: 292 (1953)

This species is accepted

The native range of this species is Tropical & Subtropical America. It is an annual or subshrub and grows primarily in the seasonally dry tropical biome. It is used as animal food and a medicine, has social uses and for food.

### According to Flora of Somalia

M. Thulin et al. Flora of Somalia, Vol. 1-4 [updated 2008] https://plants.jstor.org/collection/FLOS

Morphology General Habit
    Erect herb to 3 m tall, glabrous
Morphology Leaves
    Leaves lanceolate to elliptic, 2–13 x 0.2–4.5 cm, acute to acuminate, rarely obtuse at the apex; petiole 2–15 mm long
Morphology Reproductive morphology Inflorescences
    Flowers in upper axils, sometimes ± aggregated
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Calyx
    Sepals 4, 2–6 mm long
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Corolla
    Petals 3.5–5 mm long
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Androecium Stamens
    Stamens 8
Morphology Reproductive morphology Fruits
    Capsules 10–19 mm long, 4-ribbed, 4-angled
Morphology Reproductive morphology Seeds
    Seeds 0.3–0.4(–0.5) mm long.
Distribution
    S3 (near Faanole) widespread in tropical Africa, native in the New World.
Ecology
    Altitude c. 35 m.
Vernacular
    Fiideey-malabeey (Somali).
Note
    L. erecta has previously not been recorded from Somalia, and is still not known from Kenya. In Somalia the leaves are said to be cooked to make sauce for maize porridge.
[FSOM]

### According to Flora Zambesiaca

Onagraceae, P. H. Raven. Flora Zambesiaca 4. 1978

Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Calyx
    Sepals 4, 2–6 × 1–1·5 mm., lanceolate-acuminate.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Corolla
    Petals 3·5–5 × 2–2·5 mm., obovate.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Androecium Stamens
    Stamens 8, subequal; filaments c. 1·5 mm. long; anthers c. 0·6 mm. long, shedding pollen directly on the stigma at anthesis.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Pollen
    Pollen shed in tetrads.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Disc
    Disk not elevated, with a sunken, white-hairy nectary around the base of each epipetalous stamen.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Gynoecium Style
    Style 0·5–1 mm. long; stigma globose, 1–1·1 mm. thick, its upper 2/3 receptive.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Fruits
    Capsule 10–19 × 2–2·5 mm., glabrous, rarely puberulent, pale brown with 4 prominent dark brown ribs, sharply 4-angled with 4 nearly flat walls, irregularly and readily loculicidal, subsessile or on a pedicel up to 2 mm. long.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Seeds
    Seeds 0·3–0·4(0·5) × 0·2–0·3 mm., pluriseriate in each locule of the capsule, free, pale brown, minutely cellular-pitted, elongate-obovoid; raphe c. 1/5 the diameter of the body.
Cytology
    Chromosome number n=8.
Morphology General Habit
    Subglabrous erect herb from 3 cm. to more than 3 m., sometimes more or less woody at base, freely branched, the stems sharply angled from the decurrent leaf-bases.
Morphology Leaves
    Leaves 2–13 × 0·2–4·5 cm., lanceolate to elliptic, rarely ovate, narrowly cuneate at the base, the apex acuminate to acute, rarely obtuse; main veins 16–27 on each side of midrib; petiole 2–15 mm. long.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers
    Flowers solitary in upper axils.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Inflorescences Bracteoles
    Bracteoles c. 0·5 mm. long.

### According to Useful Plants and Fungi of Colombia

Distribution
    Biogeografic region: Amazonia, Andean, Caribbean, Pacific. Elevation range: 5–1500 m a.s.l. Native to Colombia. Colombian departments: Amazonas, Antioquia, Atlántico, Bolívar, Caldas, Caquetá, Chocó, Córdoba, Cundinamarca, Huila, La Guajira, Magdalena, Santander, Tolima, Valle del Cauca.
Habit
    Herb, Subshrub.
Conservation
    National Red List of Colombia (2021): Potential LC.
Ecology
    Habitat according IUCN Habitats Classification: forest and woodland, savanna, shrubland, native grassland, wetlands (inland), artificial - terrestrial.
Vernacular
    Clavos, Hartón
[UPFC]

### According to Flora of the Cayman Islands

George R. Proctor (2012). Flora of the Cayman Isands (Second Edition). Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

Morphology General Habit
    Erect, glabrous herb to 1 m tall, much-branched, the branches obscurely angled by the decurrent petioles
Morphology Leaves
    Leaves almost linear to narrowly or broadly lance-acuminate, 5–8 cm long, mostly 0.8–1.5 cm broad, slightly rough on the margins, the petioles 2–5 mm long. Flowers small, sessile or subsessile, the yellow petals 4–5 mm long
Morphology Reproductive morphology Fruits
    Capsule 2–3 mm in diameter; seeds about 0.4 mm long.
Distribution
    Grand Cayman. Nearly pantropical in distribution.
Ecology
    Chieﬂy in wet ditches and moist ﬁelds.
[Cayman]

Morphology Leaves
    Leaves lanceolate, sometimes ovate or elliptic, mostly 2–13 cm. long and 0.5–4.3 cm. wide, acute or subacuminate, rarely obtuse at apex; petiole 3–15 mm. long.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Calyx
    Sepals almost always 4 (5 seen only in one flower), 3–6 mm. long, 1–1.5 mm. wide.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Corolla
    Petals yellow, elliptic or obovate, 4–5 mm. long, 2–2.5 mm. wide.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Androecium Stamens
    Stamens twice as many as sepals.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Gynoecium Pistil
    Apex of ovary, supporting the 0.5–1 mm. long style, flat or only slightly raised.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Fruits
    Capsules thin-walled, 1–1.9 cm. long, 2.5–5 mm. wide; pedicels 0–8 mm. long.
Morphology Reproductive morphology Seeds
    Seeds pluriseriate in each cell, free, oblong-ellipsoid, narrow-raphed, 0.3–0.4 (–0.5) mm. long, 0.2–0.3 mm. wide, pale brown.
Figures
    Fig. 2/2, (p. 7).
Habitat
    Imperfectly known, probably various wet habitats; Speke and Grant’s specimen collected on “river bank”; near sea-level to 1100 m.
Distribution
    P T3 T4 T6 T8 widespread in tropical Africa from Senegal, the French Sudan and the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan southwards to Angola, Southern Rhodesia and Portuguese East Africaalso on the Comoro Islands, Madagascar and the Seychellesin America from Florida southwards to Brazil, Paraguay and Boliviaapparently quite absent from Asia although commonly recorded, due to misapplying the name J. erecta L. to J. suffruticosa L.
[FTEA]
